options: A Payables-specific feature unrelated to other subledgers
A shared engine, used across subledgers, that turns transactions into GL journals based on configurable rules
A report that lists overdue invoices
A manual journal entry screen in the General Ledger
questions.explain: SLA is a shared accounting engine used by Payables, Receivables, Fixed Assets, and other subledgers, driven by configurable accounting rules rather than hardcoded logic.

questions.q: What accounting entry does invoice validation typically generate?
options: Debit cash, credit accounts payable
Debit accounts payable, credit cash
Debit an expense or asset account, credit the accounts payable liability
No entry is generated at validation
questions.explain: Validating an invoice recognizes the expense/asset and the corresponding liability owed to the supplier.

questions.q: What accounting entry does a payment typically generate?
options: Debit the accounts payable liability, credit cash/bank
Debit an expense account, credit accounts payable
No entry -- payments are not accounted separately
Debit cash, credit an expense account
questions.explain: A payment clears the previously recognized liability by debiting it and crediting the cash/bank account.

questions.q: Why does a validated but unpaid invoice still show up as a liability on the balance sheet?
options: Because Payables makes an accounting error by default
Because unpaid invoices are excluded from the general ledger entirely
Because all invoices are automatically paid immediately
Because the liability is recognized at validation, separate from the payment event that later clears it
questions.explain: Validation and payment are two distinct accounting events; the liability persists until the payment event clears it.

questions.q: Why is Payables accounting built on configurable rules rather than hardcoded account numbers?
options: Because hardcoding is technically impossible in Oracle Fusion
Because the correct accounts depend on factors like ledger, business unit, and category, which a rules engine can handle consistently
Because rules are required only for tax calculations
Because configurable rules eliminate the need for a chart of accounts
questions.explain: A rules-driven engine lets one accounting method correctly handle many different combinations of ledger, business unit, and category without custom code for each.
